summary.text: Lesson 6 of Wordly Wise 3000 Book 9: fifteen words about argument and persuasion (aver, concede, proponent, oratory, vociferous, dogma), evaluation (assess, deficient, rudimentary), and influence (ascendancy, propagate, embody, impart), plus apropos and sojourn.

why.text: This is the argument lesson. Aver, concede, proponent and dogma are the vocabulary of debate — and each one carries information about how confident, how reluctant or how open the speaker is.

objectives.text: Define and use all fifteen Lesson 6 words correctly
Choose the right sense of embody, impart and propagate from context
Read verbs of admitting and asserting for the confidence they signal

parentNote.text: Built from the Lesson 6 word list, which the PDF also carries an exercise for (6A, Determining Precise Meaning) — several questions here echo that paraphrase-matching format. Dogma is the concept worth talking through: it describes how firmly a belief is HELD, not whether it is true, and that distinction is what makes the word useful.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz. Proponent is the exact opposite of Lesson 1’s detractor — worth pairing.

cards.def:
**Fitting the occasion; suitable or apt.** (adjective)
• The governor’s red, white and blue blouse seemed quite apropos for her post-election celebration.
• From the French à propos — “to the purpose”.

**Controlling influence; domination.** (noun)
• The ascendancy of the United States as a world power coincided with the decline of the British Empire.
• Ascend is inside it — ascendancy is power that has risen to the top.

**To analyze and determine the nature, value, or importance of.** (verb)
• After she assessed the storm damage, she proposed a plan.
• assessment (n): my assessment of the refrigerator showed we needed groceries.

**To declare positively; to state as the truth.** (verb)
• The lawyer averred that her client was innocent.
• Averring is stronger than saying — it stakes the speaker’s credibility on it.

**To admit to be true, often reluctantly.** (verb)
• Bungee jumpers concede that the sport can be dangerous.
• Second meaning: to grant or let have — Marla conceded the chess game.
cards.hint: The reluctance is built in. You concede what you would rather not admit.

cards.def:
**Lacking.** (adjective)
• A diet deficient in fruits and vegetables will not provide enough vitamins.
• deficiency (n): students experienced a serious deficiency when arts education was cut.

**An unproven principle or belief held to be true.** (noun)
• The danger is that a vague theory can harden into dogma.
• dogmatic (adj): overly positive and assertive about opinions, as if they were facts.

**To put an idea into a form that can be seen.** (verb)
• The painting embodies the love of a parent for a child.
• Second meaning: to make part of a system — the Bill of Rights embodies basic freedoms.

**To make known; to disclose.** (verb)
• He imparted his views so humorously that we were unsure whether to take them seriously.
• Second meaning: to bestow — the capers impart the right amount of sharpness to the sauce.

**The art of public speaking.** (noun)
• Miriam’s inspired oratory earned her the highest grade in the public-speaking class.
• orator (n): a public speaker. oratorical (adj): practising in the mirror sharpens oratorical skill.

**To reproduce, or to cause to reproduce.** (verb)
• Begonias are easy plants to propagate.
• Third meaning: to foster the spread of — he wrote articles to propagate his theory.

**Someone who proposes or supports an idea; an advocate.** (noun)
• The bill passed easily because its proponents were in the majority.
• The exact opposite of a detractor, from Lesson 1.

**Not yet fully developed; basic or elementary.** (adjective)
• The rudimentary train system developed rapidly in the later nineteenth century.
• Juan speaks four languages perfectly and has a rudimentary knowledge of several more.

**A visit or temporary stay.** (noun)
• Our summer sojourn with our cousins ended after six wonderful weeks in Puerto Rico.
• Also a verb: we sojourn for a week at our grandparents’ cabin.
cards.hint: Jour is French for day — a sojourn is measured in days, never permanent.

cards.def:
**Making one’s feelings known in a loud way.** (adjective)
• The community’s vociferous opposition to the stadium led the governor to abandon the plan.
• Voc- is voice, the same root as vocal and vocabulary.

questions.hint: From the French for "to the purpose".
steps: Apropos means fitting the occasion; suitable or apt.
A red, white and blue blouse at a post-election party is apropos — it suits the moment.
The wrong options describe cost, volume and development.

ex.main: **Fitting for the occasion.** Apropos is about suitability to a moment, not quality in general.
ex.tip: French borrowings often keep their original shape and stress. Say it ap-ruh-POH, not "a-PROP-os".

questions.q: A proponent of a plan is someone who:
questions.hint: Think of the opposite of a detractor.
steps: A proponent is someone who proposes or supports an idea; an advocate.
A bill passing because its proponents were in the majority means its supporters outnumbered its opponents.
Opposing is what an opponent or detractor does.

ex.main: **Supports and advocates for it.** Proponent and detractor (Lesson 1) are exact opposites — learn them facing each other.
ex.tip: When two lessons hand you a matched pair, link them. Pairs are cheaper to remember than singles.

questions.hint: Think of the first stage of something.
steps: Rudimentary means not yet fully developed; basic or elementary.
Juan speaking four languages perfectly and having rudimentary knowledge of several more shows the contrast.
Rudimentary knowledge is real knowledge — just early-stage, not wrong.

ex.main: **Basic and not fully developed.** Note it does NOT mean incorrect, which is the trap option.
ex.tip: Incomplete and incorrect are different claims. Tests reliably offer the wrong one as a distractor.

opts: Declare it positively as the truth
questions.hint: It is a strong, confident statement.
steps: Aver means to declare positively; to state as the truth.
A lawyer averring that her client is innocent is staking her credibility on the claim.
Doubting and asking are the opposite posture.

ex.main: **Declare it positively as the truth.** Averring is stronger than saying — the speaker is standing behind it.
ex.tip: Verbs of speaking vary by confidence: suggest, claim, assert, aver. Note where each sits on that scale.

questions.q: Vociferous opposition is opposition that is:
questions.hint: Voc- is the root for voice.
steps: Vociferous means making one's feelings known in a loud way.
A community's vociferous opposition made the governor abandon the stadium — they were heard.
The word says nothing about whether the opposition was right or well-informed.

ex.main: **Loudly expressed.** Vociferous describes volume, not validity.
ex.tip: The root voc- (voice) runs through vocal, vocabulary, advocate and vociferous.

steps: A sojourn is a visit or temporary stay.
A summer sojourn with cousins lasting six weeks is temporary by definition.
Permanence is exactly what the word rules out.

ex.main: **A temporary stay.** The French jour (day) inside it is the reminder — a sojourn is counted in days.
ex.tip: If a root you recognise contradicts an option, that option is out. Jour cannot mean permanent.

questions.q: A scientist warns that "a useful theory can harden into dogma." She is warning that the theory might:
opts: Come to be treated as unquestionable fact
Be forgotten by the next generation
questions.hint: Dogma is belief held without proof.
steps: Dogma is an unproven principle or belief held to be true.
"Hardening into dogma" means people stop treating it as a theory open to testing.
The danger is not that it is wrong — it is that it stops being questioned.

ex.main: **Treated as unquestionable fact.** The warning is about how a belief is HELD, not whether it is true.
ex.tip: Dogma is about the holder's attitude. A correct idea held dogmatically is still dogma.

questions.q: A senator "conceded that the programme had gone over budget." The word conceded tells you she:
opts: Learned it for the first time
questions.hint: Reluctance is built into the word.
steps: Concede means to admit to be true, often reluctantly.
The reluctance is part of the definition, not an inference.
So a senator conceding an overspend is admitting something she would rather not.

ex.main: **Admitted it reluctantly.** Reporters pick concede precisely because it signals the admission was pulled out.
ex.tip: Verbs of admitting carry different weights: revealed, admitted, conceded. Each implies a different amount of pressure.

questions.q: Which sentence uses embody in the book’s FIRST sense — putting an idea into visible form?
opts: The memorial embodies the grief of an entire generation
The contract embodies the terms both sides agreed
She embodied her notes into the final report
The committee embodied at noon on Tuesday
questions.hint: One sense is about making an idea visible; the other is about incorporating into a system.
steps: Embody's first sense is putting an idea into a form that can be seen.
A memorial makes an abstract grief physical and visible — that is the first sense exactly.
The contract example is the second sense (incorporating into a system), and the last two are not English usages.

ex.main: **The memorial embodies grief.** An abstract feeling is given a physical, visible form.
ex.tip: When a word has two senses, the test usually names which one it wants. Read the question stem carefully first.

steps: A proponent is someone who supports — the noun names a person by the action they perform.
So the pattern is: person : the action that defines them.
A detractor is someone who criticizes. Same pattern. Match.
Dogma lacks proof, a sojourn lacks permanence, and apropos simply means fitting.

ex.main: **Both pairs are PERSON : DEFINING ACTION.** A proponent supports; a detractor criticizes.
ex.tip: Person-to-action pairs are common and easy once named. Ask: "what does this person DO, by definition?"

questions.hint: How close are these two in meaning?
steps: Deficient means lacking — the two words are synonyms.
So the relationship is simply: same meaning.
Vociferous means loud in expressing feeling. Same meaning. Match.
Ascendancy is the opposite of decline, rudimentary is the opposite of complete, and an orator delivers a speech.

ex.main: **Both pairs are SYNONYMS.** Deficient and lacking overlap; so do vociferous and loud.
ex.tip: Two of the wrong options here are antonyms. When several options share one relationship, work out the stem first and ignore the noise.

steps: Dogma is an UNPROVEN belief held to be true — the noun names what is absent.
So the pattern is: noun : the thing it lacks.
Something rudimentary lacks full development. Match.
A proponent provides support, assessing produces judgement, and a sojourn IS a visit.

ex.main: **Both pairs are NOUN : WHAT IT LACKS.** Dogma has no proof; the rudimentary has no full development.
ex.tip: You have now seen “lacks” in four lessons with adjectives and nouns alike. The relationship travels; the part of speech does not matter.

questions.q: A commentator writes: "His oratory was superb, but his argument was rudimentary." What is the criticism?
opts: He spoke beautifully but his reasoning was underdeveloped
He spoke badly but reasoned well
He spoke too quietly to be heard
He refused to state his position
questions.hint: The two halves of the sentence are pulling in opposite directions.
steps: Oratory is the art of public speaking, so "superb oratory" praises his delivery.
Rudimentary means basic and not fully developed, applied here to his argument.
The "but" sets them against each other: the performance was excellent, the thinking was not.

ex.main: **Beautiful delivery, underdeveloped reasoning.** The sentence separates HOW he spoke from WHAT he said — which is the whole point of having both words.
ex.tip: A "but" between two clauses is a signpost. The writer is telling you the two halves do not match.

questions.q: Which sentence shows propagate in its "foster the spread of" sense rather than its biological sense?
opts: He wrote several articles to propagate his theory about climate change
Begonias are easy plants to propagate from cuttings
The frogs that propagated in the fall had few offspring
The gardener propagated the roses successfully
questions.hint: One of these spreads an idea; the others spread organisms.
steps: Propagate means to reproduce or cause to reproduce, and also to foster the spread of something.
Articles written to spread a theory use the third sense — spreading an idea, not offspring.
Begonias, frogs and roses are all the biological sense.

ex.main: **Writing articles to spread a theory.** The same verb covers reproducing plants and spreading ideas — both are about multiplying and spreading.
ex.tip: When one word covers a literal and a figurative sense, find the shared motion. Here it is "spreading widely".

steps: Ascendancy means controlling influence; domination.
The ascendancy of the United States as a world power coinciding with Britain's decline is the book's example.
The climbing image is where the word comes from, but the meaning is about power, not physical height.

ex.main: **Controlling influence or domination.** Ascendancy is power that has risen to the top and holds it.
ex.tip: A word can keep the picture of its root while leaving the literal meaning behind.

questions.q: A city "assessed the damage" after a flood. This means officials:
opts: Analyzed it to determine its nature and extent
steps: Assess means to analyze and determine the nature, value or importance of something.
Assessing storm damage before proposing a plan is the book's example — evaluation comes first.
Repairing, blaming and reporting are all things that might FOLLOW an assessment.

ex.main: **Analyzed it to determine its nature and extent.** Assessment is the measuring step, not the fixing step.
ex.tip: Sequence words matter in reports: assess, then plan, then act. Mixing up the stage changes the claim.

questions.q: A chef says the herbs "impart a subtle flavour." Impart here means to:
questions.hint: Impart has two senses. Which fits herbs and flavour?
steps: Impart means to make known or disclose, and also to bestow.
Herbs cannot disclose anything — they GIVE flavour to a dish.
The book's own example is capers imparting sharpness to a sauce.

ex.main: **Give or bestow.** The disclosure sense needs a speaker; the bestowing sense works for ingredients.
ex.tip: For two-sense words, ask whether the subject can perform the action. Herbs cannot reveal secrets.

questions.q: A critic writes that a politician is "dogmatic about policies she once held tentatively." What has changed?
opts: She now asserts as certain what she previously treated as open to question
She has abandoned the policies entirely
She has become better informed about them
She now keeps her views private
questions.hint: Dogmatic describes how firmly a belief is held.
steps: Dogmatic means overly positive and assertive about opinions, as if they were facts.
Holding something tentatively means treating it as provisional, open to revision.
So the change is in CERTAINTY, not in the content of the policies.
She has moved from provisional to unquestionable without the evidence necessarily changing.

ex.main: **She now asserts as certain what she once held provisionally.** The policies may be identical; the certainty is not.
ex.tip: A criticism can target how a belief is held rather than what it says. That is a subtler and often fairer attack.
